## The future: towards a drier and warmer climate?

The figures handled by the technicians at the District Agricultural Office of Órgiva leave no room for skepticism. According to the report 'Climate Change in Andalusia', prepared by the Junta, AEMET models for the most unfavorable scenario, RCP 8.5, project an increase of 2.5 degrees Celsius in the average temperature of the Alpujarra by 2050. Precipitation, meanwhile, would fall by twenty percent compared to historical records. These are figures that, translated to the ground, mean a profound alteration of the bioclimatic zones that have organized life in these mountains for centuries.

The supramediterranean zone, that band where chestnut trees and Pyrenean oaks find their optimal humidity, would shift from the current 1,200 meters of Pampaneira up to 1,600. Capileira, at 1,436 meters, would be trapped in a drier climatic step, more akin to the one the towns of the lower Alpujarra endure today. The difference may seem like a botanical technicality, but it entails concrete decisions about which fruit tree varieties will survive, which dryland crops will cease to make sense, and which slopes will be exposed to a fire risk that has already claimed thousands of hectares on the southern slope of Sierra Nevada.

Farmers are not waiting for the models to be confirmed. On experimental farms in the Guadalfeo basin, several producers have begun planting pistachios at altitudes where a decade ago no one would have considered them viable. The pistachio tree requires dry heat in summer and sufficient winter cold, a combination that previously only occurred in the lower, more arid areas of the province. Its presence now on slopes at 1,100 or 1,200 meters is a vegetal thermometer that confirms, with shoots and leaves, what satellites record in degrees Celsius.

The avocado, the star crop of the Granada tropical coast, is also moving uphill. Where dryland almond trees or mountain vineyards were once planted, terraces now appear with Hass variety avocados, demanding in water but profitable as long as the aquifers hold out. The paradox is evident: the crop that best adapts to the new climate is precisely the one that exerts the most pressure on an increasingly scarce water resource. The technicians at the District Agricultural Office summarize it with a phrase circulating among irrigators: "The avocado goes up because the climate goes up, but the water doesn't go up with it."

The issue of water runs through any conversation about the future of the region. The acequias de careo, that centuries-old system that recharges aquifers by filtering meltwater down the slopes, depend on snow that arrives later and melts earlier each year. If the snow line rises another two hundred meters, as projections suggest, the recharge mechanism will weaken just when crops demand more irrigation. It is a mismatch that farmers sense in the calendar: sowings are brought forward, harvests overlap, and late frosts, once predictable, have become a lottery.

The towns of the high Alpujarra, accustomed to looking towards Sierra Nevada as an inexhaustible reservoir of water and coolness, are beginning to contemplate a different horizon. Summers are lengthening, and tropical nights—those where the thermometer does not drop below twenty degrees—are ceasing to be a rarity in July to also appear in August and even September. Rural tourism, which has sustained the region's economy over the last two decades, is noticing the change in demand: visitors are asking for houses with swimming pools, something unthinkable in traditional Alpujarra architecture, and hiking routes are concentrated in the early hours of the morning.

The Junta de Andalucía has incorporated these scenarios into its adaptation plans, but the scale of the challenge overflows any administrative document. It is not just a matter of replacing some crops with others or reinforcing irrigation infrastructure. It is about deciding whether the Alpujarra we know—that succession of green terraces, centuries-old chestnut trees, and white villages clinging to the mountainside—can be maintained when the climate that made it possible shifts uphill. The data is on the table. The decisions, for now, are advancing more slowly than the mercury in the thermometer.
